1 · The market

Part 1

How one auction sets 24 prices a day, the file, a price per year, prices below zero, and a year hour by hour.

The day-ahead auction

At noon today one auction sets all 24 of tomorrow’s prices, and today’s are already known. The forecast in the file comes out at 18:00 and stands in for a bidder’s own.

The merit order play

The offers are stacked from cheapest to most expensive, and the last one needed sets the price for all. Wind bids near zero; the blocks are stylised.

Reading the file

The table has 26,133 rows, one per hour from 2022 to 2024. With time as the index, .loc picks out a day, a month or a year.

The columns

price the day-ahead price in West Denmark, kroner per MWh wind the forecast of wind output, MW
date the day, as text: 2024-10-04 solar the forecast of solar output, MW
hour the clock hour, 0 to 23 time the index: the hour, Danish time
weekday 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday weekend 1 on a Saturday or a Sunday

Seven days with no published forecast are left out. On the day the clocks go forward there are 23 hours, and on the day they go back the repeated hour is averaged.

A price per year

The average hour cost 1,630 kroner in 2022 and 531 in 2024, a fall of two thirds. The most expensive hour, at 17:00 on 12 December 2024, cost 6,982.

Prices below zero

The price was below zero in 360 hours of 2024, so buyers were paid to take the power; the lowest, in July 2023, was 3,277 kroner below zero.

Hours above or below a price play

Slide the price and switch between below and above. Above 1,000 kroner there were 6,086 hours in 2022, and 525 in 2024.

2024, hour by hour play

Each column is a day of 2024 and each row an hour. Step through the days or click one to draw its 24 prices; the dark bands are the daily peaks.

2 · Why the price moves

Part 2

The hour of the day, the month, the wind, today against tomorrow, and the size of the moves from one day to the next.

The shape of a day

The average price peaks at 08:00 and 19:00, when demand peaks, and is lowest at 03:00 and 14:00.

The shape, month by month play

Step through the months, and switch between weekdays and weekends. At weekends the morning peak almost disappears: 08:00 averages 777 kroner, against 1,274.

Wind, sun and the price play

More wind lowers the median price in every year. The sun lowers it only when strong: above 1,000 MW the median is 348 kroner, against 722 with no sun.

Today and tomorrow play

More wind tomorrow is blue, and so is a lower price, so the two panels mostly line up. On Monday 8 January they do not, and every hour rose.

Daily moves, power against the S&P 500

The day’s average price moved more than 20 percent from the day before on 204 days of 2024. The S&P 500’s largest daily move that year was 3.0 percent.

Your turn 1

Fill a dictionary with the median price at 03:00, 08:00, 13:00 and 18:00, then get all 24 medians in one line with groupby.

Your turn 1: answer

medians = {}
for h in [3, 8, 13, 18]:
    medians[h] = power[power['hour'] == h]['price'].median()
    print(h, medians[h])

print(power.groupby('hour')['price'].median())
3 626.47
8 844.57
13 550.56
18 895.19

The mask inside the loop keeps one hour at a time, and groupby does all 24 at once. The median at 18:00 is 43 percent above the median at 03:00.

3 · A first classifier

Part 3

The question from your forecasts as a label, a rule of thumb, the weekday as seven columns, and today’s move.

The same hour, one day earlier

Within each hour, shift(1) moves the prices down one row, so each row gets the day before’s price. Returns within each ticker were built the same way.

The label

An hour’s label up is 1 when it costs more than the same hour the day before. The first day of the table has no day before, so its price_before is empty.

The wind change

wind_change is tomorrow’s wind forecast minus today’s. When it falls by more than 1,000 MW, 86 percent of hours rise; when it rises that much, 12 percent.

The logistic curve play

The dots are the share of hours that rose, and the red curve is a logistic regression on the wind change. Drag the slider to read its probability.

The weekday, as one number or seven columns play

 AUC on 2024

As one number, the weekday can only tilt the week one way. As seven columns, each day gets its own level, and the dots sit on the bars.

Weekday columns in code

get_dummies turns the weekday into seven columns of zeros and ones, and the loop copies each into the table and keeps its name. On every row exactly one of them is 1.

Today’s move

shift(2) reaches two days back, so change_before is today’s move. After a fall of over 200 kroner, 60 percent of hours rise; after such a rise, 42.

The rows to learn from

dropna removes the first two days, which have no day before. Calling no hour of 2024 up, the majority rule, is right 50.3 percent of the time.

A rule of thumb

The rule says up whenever tomorrow’s wind forecast is lower than today’s. It is right 71.9 percent of the time in 2024, against 50.3 for the majority rule.

Logistic regression on the wind change

With one column the model ranks the hours in the same order as the wind change itself: an AUC of 0.796. What it adds is a probability for every hour.

Adding columns one kind at a time

Each step adds one kind of column, and the AUC rises from 0.796 to 0.833. After the loop, p holds the probabilities of the last model, the one with all three.

Choose the columns play

AUC on the folds of 2022 and 2023, where the columns are chosen. Dashed: the model on the slides.

Tick the columns the model may use; each tick shows what it adds on the folds of 2022 and 2023. The dashed line is the model on the slides.

C on the folds

The folds move forward in time. Every C from 0.01 to 10 scores 0.815 on them, so the penalty barely matters here.

C, as a slider play

A small C pulls every coefficient toward zero and the probabilities toward one half. At 0.0001 the ranking barely changes, but the Brier score rises from 0.167 to 0.211.

The confusion matrix

At one half the model catches 3,171 of the 4,303 hours that rose, a recall of 0.737. When it says up, it is right 74.5 percent of the time.

Predictions and mistakes, 2024 play

On 143 of 2024’s 361 days, at least 20 of the 24 hours moved the same way. The model was right on 85 percent of those hours, and on 68 percent of the others.

The same question for the S&P 500

74.4%
power, 2024: hours called right by the model
50.3%
power, 2024: the majority rule
50.4%
S&P 500, 2024: days called right from yesterday’s return and the weekday
58.7%
S&P 500, 2024: always saying up

A share can be bought today and sold tomorrow, so a rise anyone can predict is bought away before it happens. Power cannot be stored in bulk, so tomorrow’s hour is a different good.

4 · What it is worth

Part 4

A bet on the direction of every hour, the kroner in each cell of the confusion matrix, and a threshold set by the cost of trading.

A bet on the direction

For each hour of 2024, bet 1 MWh on the direction: long when the probability is high, short when it is low. Each trade earns the move and pays a cost of 50 kroner.

The move in each hour

Knowing every direction in advance, with no cost, would earn 1,868,568 kroner in 2024. Always going long earns 514, because the rises and falls almost cancel.

A function for the P&L

At one half every hour is traded, and the model earns 879,112 kroner after costs. At 0.6 the hours near one half are left out, and it earns 957,809.

The threshold, in kroner play

Each trade earns or loses the move and pays 50 kroner. At 0.64 the model trades 6,225 of the 8,663 hours and earns 975,120 kroner, the most of any threshold.

The cost of trading play

The best threshold rises with the cost: 0.53 with no cost, 0.64 at 50 kroner and 0.77 at 150. At 150, one half earns 12,812 kroner and 0.77 earns 468,445.

Your turn 2

Choose the threshold on 2022 and 2023 instead, at a cost of 50. Fill earned with what pnl gives on the training rows at each threshold, and find the best.

Your turn 2: answer

earned = {}
for t in [0.5, 0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7]:
    earned[t] = pnl(p_train, move_train, t, 50)
print(earned)
# {0.5: 3276105, 0.55: 3354200, 0.6: 3340692, 0.65: 3284499, 0.7: 3157485}

On 2022 and 2023, 0.55 earns the most, and in 2024 it earns 928,247 kroner. That is 95 percent of the best threshold in hindsight, 0.64 with 975,120.

What the P&L leaves out

The cost of 50 kroner per MWh is a round number for fees and the bid-ask spread, not a measured one.

The size of 1 MWh moves no price. A large bet placed in the auction would move the price against itself.

The contract that pays the change from one day to the next at one hour does not exist. The bet stands in for a buyer who can move use between days.

The forecast in the file comes out at 18:00, after the auction, so the model saw a slightly better forecast than a bidder has.

5 · The crisis in the training rows

Part 5

A second label on the level of the price, an hour above 1,000 kroner, fitted with and without 2022, and its probabilities checked against 2024.

Prices above 1,000 kroner

In 2022, 70 percent of the hours cost more than 1,000 kroner, and in 2024, 6 percent. The share that rose from the day before stayed near half in every year.

Two training windows

With 2022 and 2023 the model expects 40 percent of 2024’s hours above 1,000 kroner, and with 2023 alone 13; the share was 6.

Predicted against actual play

Each dot is a group of 2024’s hours. With 2022 in training, a probability near 0.3 meant 0.8 percent; with 2023 alone, 15 percent.

AUC against the Brier score

Both models rank 2024’s hours equally well, with AUCs of 0.839 and 0.838. Only the Brier score shows the difference: 0.187 against 0.062.

Handling a changed market

A recent window 2023 alone forecast 2024 better than 2022 and 2023 together: a Brier score of 0.062 against 0.187.

Watch the average Compare the mean probability with the share that happened, month by month, and retrain when the gap grows.

A label that travels The direction model, trained on the same years, gave 2024 an average probability of 0.495; the share that rose was 0.497.

6 · Similar hours

Part 6

Three classes, a big move either way, the k most similar hours of the past, a feature lab, and your forecasts revised and scored.

Three classes

pd.cut makes three classes: more than 50 kroner down, less than 50 either way, and more than 50 up. The majority rule scores 0.381 and the model 0.606.

The three-class confusion matrix

Rows are what happened, from lower to higher. The model never predicts about the same: in no hour of 2024 is it the most likely of the three.

A big move either way play

 AUC on 2024

A move of more than 150 kroner is most likely when the wind forecast changes a lot, either way. A logistic regression on the wind change can only slope one way.

The size of the wind change

abs builds the size of the wind change, a shape a linear model cannot make from the change itself. The AUC for a big move rises from 0.559 to 0.670.

The k nearest hours play

k-NN finds the k hours of 2022 and 2023 most like this one and reports the share that rose. Untick the scaler, and the weekday stops counting.

k-NN in code

k-NN needs no weekday columns: the nearest hours to a Monday are Mondays. With k of 201, chosen on the folds, it scores 0.844 against the logistic regression’s 0.833.

k-NN without the scaler

Without the scaler the AUC falls to 0.797, since the wind change spreads over thousands of megawatts and the weekday over seven values.

The feature lab play

AUC on the folds of 2022 and 2023, where the columns are chosen. Dashed: the model on the slides.

The same columns for k-NN, and for a big move either way. The dashed lines are the models on the slides, and they can be beaten.

The scoreboard

Both scores are losses, so lower is better. The log loss punishes a confident wrong answer hardest, as on 2 January.

Everything used today

Looking at a market read_csv with parse_dates, set_index, .loc by date, groupby by year and by hour, pd.cut into bands, a bar chart and two lines.

Loops, dictionaries, functions A dictionary of medians filled by a loop, a loop that adds the weekday columns, a ladder of models in a dictionary, and pnl on two sets of rows.

A label from the day before shift(1) inside groupby('hour') puts the same hour of the day before on every row. About half the hours rose, in every year.

Columns built from others The wind change gave an AUC of 0.796, the weekday as seven columns 0.830, and today’s move 0.833.

The threshold and the cost The best threshold rose with the cost. Chosen on 2022 and 2023, 0.55 earned 928,247 kroner in 2024 at 50 kroner a trade.

Training rows from another market Trained through 2022, the model expected 40 percent of 2024’s hours above 1,000 kroner. The share was 6 percent.

A shape a line cannot make The size of the wind change took a big move’s AUC from 0.559 to 0.670, and k-NN found the shape by itself.

k-NN and the scoreboard The weekday and the hour as plain numbers, scaled: an AUC of 0.844. On your eight hours k-NN scored 0.166 and logistic regression 0.194.
